content: Ivermectin, administered as an oral dose under the Mectizan Donation Program, has been shown to temporarily reduce the skin microfilarial load of Onchocerca volvulus to levels below those required for effective transmission by Simulium species (black flies). This drug also exhibits microfilarial suppressive activity in adult female worms and has a detrimental effect on adult worms, particularly when administered multiple times per year. Studies conducted in endemic onchocerciasis regions in Africa and the Americas have demonstrated that sustained, high-level coverage with ivermectin is essential for successfully controlling transmission and reducing morbidity. An important criterion for evaluating a country’s control program is evidence of broad and effective ivermectin coverage sustained over a sufficiently long period to interrupt transmission and reduce morbidity. Onchocerciasis control programs implementing mass drug administration (MDA) with ivermectin typically progress through three phases: the intervention or treatment phase, post-treatment surveillance, and post-elimination surveillance. During the first phase, regular ivermectin treatment is administered, requiring at least 80% therapeutic coverage of the eligible population in each treatment round. This phase, lasting 12–15 years with annual treatment, corresponds to the reproductive lifespan of the adult parasite under drug pressure. By the end of this phase, most adult worms should have died or become infertile. However, some adult worms or microfilariae may persist, but the minimal level of transmission that may occur will not sustain the parasite population, indicating that elimination is imminent. At this point, the program may decide to suspend treatment. The second phase, post-treatment surveillance, begins when interventions are stopped. During this period, periodic assessments are conducted to confirm that transmission remains interrupted for at least 3–5 years, depending on the specific parameters of each focus. This phase is particularly critical in areas at high risk of infection recrudescence, such as those with historically high infection prevalence, low treatment coverage, or political instability. Assessments may be conducted by focus, transmission zone, or country, and isolated foci may be evaluated at different times if MDA activities are not synchronized. Diagnostic tests used during post-treatment surveillance must be statistically robust and include validated sample sizes of vectors and/or affected human populations. Entomological evaluation using the O-150 PCR technique is a key diagnostic method to determine the presence of infective-stage O. volvulus larvae in vector populations. Black flies are collected during peak transmission seasons, pooled by collection site, and analyzed for the presence of parasite DNA. Positive results in fly bodies, which may contain immature larval stages, do not necessarily indicate ongoing transmission, as infective-stage larvae (L3) must be present in the vector’s head to confirm transmission. Serological evaluation using the O. volvulus Ov-16 antibody test is another valuable tool. This minimally invasive test detects IgG4 antibodies to the Ov-16 antigen, indicating exposure to the parasite. A sample size of 2,000 children under 10 years of age is typically required to meet statistical criteria. However, serologically positive children who test negative for patent infection via PCR testing of skin snips are considered uninfected. These children should be retested after 1–2 years to confirm their status. Parasitological evaluation using skin snip microscopy and the DEC patch test remains useful for monitoring progress during the treatment phase. However, a test capable of detecting new patent infections with high positive predictive value is still needed. Efforts are ongoing to develop such tests, which will be incorporated into program evaluations as they become available. The original 2001 WHO guidelines for certifying the elimination of human onchocerciasis included criteria such as the absence or near absence of infective-stage O. volvulus in vectors and the absence of detectable infection in untreated children or new residents in endemic areas. These criteria have since been operationalized in Latin America and Africa, with elimination achieved in several countries. The updated guidelines aim to provide evidence-based recommendations for discontinuing MDA and verifying the elimination of O. volvulus transmission, adhering to WHO standards for guideline development.
